PART 15 — SHARING THE RELATIONAL GOSPEL WITH AN UNBELIEVER

15.1 Why the Starting Point Changes

A traditional transactional presentation often starts with guilt and the danger of punishment. The relational gospel, as this whole series has developed it, starts with identity and inclusion: you were made for union with God; something broke it (sin, the I-am-nots entering by belief, Part 1.2); Jesus came, as true humanity united to God in one person, to undo it from the inside and include us in what he has with the Father.

An evenhanded note. Both framings are held by sincere, faithful Christians across traditions. Forensic and substitutionary accounts of the atonement (Christ's death satisfying justice, paying a penalty) are historic, widely affirmed, and well-supported scripturally (e.g. Rom 3:25; 2 Cor 5:21; 1 Pet 2:24). The relational/inclusion framing associated with Kruger and the wider Torrance tradition complements this for many believers rather than replacing it, though some other Christians raise concerns that language of universal inclusion can blur into universalism if not carefully qualified. This document does not resolve that debate; it simply uses the relational framing consistently, as the rest of this series has, because that is the lens requested.

15.2 A Practical Sequence, Built From Everything in This Study

  1. Listen first; diagnose nothing aloud. Use Part 4's NVC pattern — observe, ask about feeling and need — before offering any content. Ask about their story, their picture of God, their history with religion.
  2. Locate the wound behind the resistance. Most resistance to "God" is wound-based, not purely intellectual — often resistance to a false, Babylonian picture of God (Part 1.2's "upstream" distorted God-picture) or a bad experience with Christians (Part 3.4 and Part 7.7's Babylon vs. Kingdom distinction). Respond to the actual wound honestly; do not defend institutional failure.
  3. Present God's character accurately before any content. The Father who ran to the prodigal before the rehearsed confession finished (Luke 15:20) — not a distant, demanding God. Most resistance to "God" dissolves somewhat once the actual God in view is corrected.
  4. Share your own story, briefly. One real I-am-not met by Christ (Part 3.3's confession, applied evangelistically) — testimony before argument.
  5. Offer the core content simply: made for union with God → separated by sin and the lies we came to believe about ourselves → Jesus came and undid it from the inside, uniting true humanity to God → the invitation is to trust and receive, not to perform or earn.
  6. Make it a request, not a demand (Part 4.2 — Rev 3:20, "I stand at the door and knock"). Respect their freedom fully; no pressure tactics, no urgency manufactured artificially.
  7. Tailor to their actual case: if they seem to carry no felt need (Part 14), frame it as invitation and fulfilment; if they carry an active wound, let Part 1's gospel-answers-to-I-am-nots and Part 3's shame material shape the content; if they were hurt by Christians, be honest about Babylon vs. Kingdom rather than defensive.

15.3 A Sample Dialogue (illustrative, composite)

Them: "I'm not really into religion. I had a rough time with church growing up — lots of rules, not much love."

You: "That sounds painful. Can I ask what it felt like, growing up in that?"

Them: "Like I always had to earn approval. Nothing was ever enough."

You: "I'm sorry that's what you experienced. For what it's worth, that version doesn't match what I understand the actual gospel to be — a God who runs toward people before they've cleaned anything up. I used to believe something similar to what you just described about myself, that I wasn't enough, and what changed it wasn't trying harder, it was realising that wasn't actually God's verdict on me. I'm not trying to convince you of anything right now — just wanted you to know that what you experienced and what I'm talking about aren't the same thing."

15.4 What Not to Do — Babylon's Evangelism Counterfeits

Counterfeit tacticWhat it actually does
Fear-based urgency ("you could die tonight")Manufactures crisis rather than inviting genuine trust; produces compliance, not relationship
Shame-based guilt inductionAdds a new I-am-not ("I am not good enough to be forgiven") rather than removing one
Argument-only approachIgnores the wound behind the resistance (Part 15.2, step 2); wins a debate, loses the person
Conditional warmth ("we'll really welcome you once you believe/behave")Exactly the performance-based love this whole series has named as counterfeit (Part 5.5, Part 6.5)
Scripture used to win rather than to loveViolates the NVC limits named in Part 4.2-4.3 — truth without the care that should carry it

15.5 One-Page Summary

Listen before speaking. Name the real God before naming sin. Share your story before your argument. Invite, never pressure. Tailor the frame — rescue for the wounded, fulfilment for the secure — to the actual person in front of you, not a script. The goal is not to win an argument or close a transaction; it is to introduce a person to a Father who has already been running toward them.

PART 16 — Practical Toolkit, Trackers and FAQ

16.1 Self-Check Questions (for reflection, not diagnosis)

  • Which I-am-nots do I hear when overlooked or criticized? (family: belonging, security, significance, performance, standing before God)
  • Which of the five methods do I reach for first? Which when it's too much?
  • What picture of God do I carry when I fail — watching, distant, demanding, or loving?
  • Do I lean Defender or Seeker? Do I switch by setting?
  • Can I receive correction, celebrate others, and forgive without great effort?

16.2 The Seven-Step Practice (from Kruger's pathway, Part 3.5, applied generally)

  1. Name the verdict in plain words.
  2. See which method you reached for.
  3. Look at your God-picture in that moment.
  4. Meet Jesus inside it — sit with the I-am-not in his presence.
  5. Agree and reckon — say the Father's verdict aloud and let it count as true.
  6. Take his side against the old story — then act (have the conversation, set the boundary, forgive).
  7. Live it with others, in community where you are seen.

16.4 Frequently Asked Questions

QuestionAnswer
Does everyone really have I-am-nots?Nearly everyone, in different strengths — see Part 1.5. Not everyone needs intensive heart-healing.
Isn't naming "toxic traits" just labeling people?The traits describe patterns, not permanent identities (Part 7.4). The question is pattern, severity, and willingness to change.
How is confession different from confronting exploitation?Confession (Part 3) is agreeing with God/a safe person about your own wrong. Confronting exploitation (Part 5.4) is naming someone else's wrong to you. Both use the same NVC structure (Part 4) but serve different purposes.
Why does the sibling study matter for a marriage problem?Because the cover (control, stonewalling, clinging) was usually rehearsed first in the family of origin — see Part 9.2.
What if I recognize myself as the Defender/controller in these pages?Seeking help is courage, not defeat (Part 7.4's closing note). Christ meets people inside their I-am-nots; change is still a choice that takes accountable steps over time.
What's the one-sentence difference between an unmet need and an I-am-not?A need is a legitimate hunger that circumstances left unmet; an I-am-not is the false verdict about identity that sometimes — not always — forms in response (Part 11.1).
Can I really become unoffendable?Functionally and progressively, yes — not as an instant switch, but as fewer I-am-nots remain for an insult to hook onto (Part 13.2). Full immunity this side of glory is not typically claimed even by mature believers.
If someone had a genuinely healthy childhood, do they even need the gospel?Yes — the gospel's core claim (reconciliation, inclusion in the Trinity's life, meaning beyond self-management) is not conditional on anyone's wound history. See Part 14.

Scripture is cited throughout for study; interpretations, the Defender/Seeker framework, the I-am-not "families," the case studies (all marked composite unless drawn from named Scripture figures), and the integration across all sixteen parts are synthesis — the uploaded source documents' own synthesis where noted, and this document's synthesis where it draws connections between those sources and the earlier studies in this conversation, including the needs-vs-I-am-not distinction (Part 11), the treatment of anger and offense (Parts 12-13), and the evangelism material (Part 15). NVC is Marshall Rosenberg's framework; its Christological reading is the source author's own. Indian helpline numbers and the 2005 Act are as described by the Ministry of Women and Child Development; verify current details locally. Christians disagree on divorce/remarriage, on women's roles in ministry, and on how substitutionary and relational/inclusion models of the atonement relate to each other (Part 15.1); this document notes those disagreements rather than resolving them.
